hints: Focus on the clue that methylamine behaves very like ammonia, so its salt should behave very like ammonium chloride.
Recall what happens when ammonium chloride, $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$, is warmed with $\text{NaOH}$, it releases the free base $\text{NH}_3$ plus $\text{NaCl}$ and $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.
Now swap $\text{NH}_3$ for $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ in that same pattern to predict which three products must form together.
walkthrough:
**Recall the familiar ammonia test**

Think of this as a friend of a reaction you already know. Ammonium salts release ammonia when warmed with alkali.

$$\text{NH}_4^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{NH}_3 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

**Use the similarity given in the question**

The question tells you $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$ is very similar to $\text{NH}_3$. So $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^-$ will act just like $\text{NH}_4^+\text{Cl}^-$.

The $\text{OH}^-$ from $\text{NaOH}$ removes the extra $\text{H}^+$ from the cation to reform the free base.

**Write the parallel equation**

Just replace ammonia with methylamine in the same pattern.

$$\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{NaCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$$

So the products are methylamine, sodium chloride and water.

options.A: Incorrect. This is the product set for ordinary ammonium chloride with NaOH. Here the starting cation contains a methyl group, so the base released must be $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2$, not $\text{NH}_3$.
options.B: Incorrect. There is no source of carbon dioxide or carbonate here to make sodium hydrogencarbonate, $\text{NaHCO}_3$. This option also wrongly gives ammonia instead of methylamine.
options.C: Incorrect. Hydrogen chloride, $\text{HCl}$, cannot survive with sodium hydroxide present, it would be neutralised. The chloride ends up as $\text{NaCl}$ and the $\text{OH}^-$ ends up as water.
options.D: Correct. By analogy to $\text{NH}_4\text{Cl} + \text{NaOH}$, the hydroxide deprotonates the methylammonium ion: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_3^+ + \text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O}$, leaving $\text{Na}^+$ and $\text{Cl}^-$ to form $\text{NaCl}$.
